items.followUp: What does the prefix micro- mean? Give its value as a power of ten.

rubric.why: Defines what prefixes indicate in measurement.
rubric.description: Defines prefixes as additions before units that indicate multiples or submultiples.

rubric.why: Gives a valid prefix and its value.
rubric.description: Provides one correct example of a prefix.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any correct prefix-value example.

modelAnswer: Prefixes are symbols placed before units to indicate their multiples or submultiples.

items.followUp: Convert an age of 12 years into seconds. Take 1 year = 365 days.

rubric.why: Shows the correct conversion factors from years to seconds.
rubric.description: Uses 1 year = 365 days and 1 day = 86,400 seconds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the conversion factors.

rubric.why: Checks the calculated age in seconds.
rubric.description: Obtains the correct answer with the SI unit.

modelAnswer: Given: age = 14 years; 1 year = 365 days; 1 day = 24 × 60 × 60 s.
Formula: time in seconds = number of years × 365 × 24 × 60 × 60.

items.followUp: What is meant by the displacement of an object?

rubric.why: Position is specified relative to a reference point.
rubric.description: Defines position as the location of a body with respect to a reference point.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a clear definition.

modelAnswer: The position of a body is its location with respect to a reference point.

items.followUp: State the value of gravitational acceleration on the Moon.

rubric.why: Identifies gravitational acceleration as acceleration caused by gravity.
Checks the accepted approximate value and SI unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the value with unit.

modelAnswer: Gravitational acceleration is the acceleration of a freely falling body due to gravity.
Its value near Earth's surface is g = 9.8 m/s².

items.followUp: Write the formula for the coefficient of friction and name the forces in it.

rubric.why: Identifies the two quantities used to define the coefficient.
rubric.description: States that it is the ratio of frictional force to normal reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio.

modelAnswer: The coefficient of friction is the ratio of frictional force to normal reaction.
Its symbol is μ; μ = frictional force / normal reaction.

items.followUp: Define the pivot of a lever and the effort arm.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the line along which the force acts.
rubric.description: Defines the line of action of a force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the line along which the force acts.

rubric.why: Identifies the moment arm as a perpendicular distance from the turning axis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct distance and reference.

modelAnswer: The line of action of a force is the straight line along which the force acts.
The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot or axis of rotation to the line of action.

items.followUp: Write the formula for the moment of force and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Checks the defining product for moment of force.
rubric.description: Defines moment of force as force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from the pivot.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition or formula.

rubric.why: Checks the classification of moment of force.
rubric.description: States that moment of force is a vector quantity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a vector.

modelAnswer: The moment of force is the product of a force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot: moment = force × moment arm.
Moment of force is a vector quantity.

items.followUp: Give an example of a body in motion that is not in equilibrium, and explain why.

rubric.why: Provides a suitable example of a body momentarily at rest.
rubric.description: Names a ball or stone at the highest point of its upward motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example.

rubric.why: Explains that a non-zero resultant force means the body is not in equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that gravity still acts, so the body has a downward acceleration or unbalanced weight.

modelAnswer: A ball thrown vertically upward is momentarily at rest at its highest point.
It is not in equilibrium because gravity still acts on it, giving it a downward acceleration.
